questions.question:
You have a container in an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL account.  
  
You need to create an alert using a custom Log Analytics query.  
  
Which signal type should you use?
questions.explanation:
Azure Monitor log search alerts evaluate Log Analytics queries on a schedule and trigger when the query results meet the alert condition. This corresponds to the Log signal type.\
\
**Learn more:** [Tutorial: Create a log search alert for an Azure resource](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/alerts/tutorial-log-alert)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure Cosmos DB database that contains a container named `container1`.  
  
You need to make sure items stored in `container1` do **not** expire unless their TTL value is explicitly configured.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Set the DefaultTimeToLive property to null.

questions.explanation:
Setting `DefaultTimeToLive` to `-1` enables TTL with no default expiration. Items without an explicit TTL remain indefinitely, while an item with a positive TTL value expires according to that value. A `null` or removed container TTL disables TTL entirely and causes item-level TTL values to be ignored.

**Learn more:** [Time-To-Live (TTL) in Azure Cosmos DB](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cosmos-db/time-to-live) · [ContainerProperties.DefaultTimeToLive Property](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.azure.cosmos.containerproperties.defaulttimetolive?view=azure-dotnet)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL account that contains a database named DB1 and a container named Container1.  
  
You need to manage the account by using the Azure Cosmos DB SDK.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: List the physical partitions of Container1.
Read a stored procedure in Container1.
Create a user defined function (UDF) in Container1.

questions.explanation:
The Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL SDK exposes container/item and server-side programming resources as first-class operations, so creating a container in a database (A), reading a stored procedure in a container (C), and creating a user-defined function in a container (D) are all standard SDK calls documented in the DP-420 developer content. Listing the physical partitions of a container (B) is not a management operation surfaced by the SDK object model; physical partitioning is an internal, service-managed concern (the SDK only exposes logical feed ranges), so it is excluded. Therefore the SDK-supported management actions are A, C, and D.

**Learn more:** [Create and use a UDF with the SDK (DP-420 lab)](https://microsoftlearning.github.io/dp-420-cosmos-db-dev/instructions/33-create-use-udf-sdk.html) · [DP-420 study guide](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/credentials/certifications/resources/study-guides/dp-420)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You plan to build an operational system that stores data in an Azure Cosmos DB Core (SQL) API account.  
  
You need to configure the account to meet these requirements:  
  
- Support Spark queries.  
- Support analysis of data from the previous six months.

Which three actions should you take? Each correct answer represents part of the solution.  
  
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

options.text: Enable Azure Synapse Link for the account.
Create a container and set the analyticalTTL property to six months.
Create an Azure Synapse linked service.
Create a container and set the time to live to six months.

Azure Synapse Link exposes the Azure Cosmos DB analytical store to Azure Synapse runtimes, including Apache Spark, enabling analysis without ETL. The container’s analytical TTL controls how long data remains in that analytical store, so it must be set to six months. A Synapse linked service connects Synapse Spark to the Azure Cosmos DB database; a pipeline or Databricks notebook is not required for this configuration. lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to create a data store for a directory of small and medium-sized businesses (SMBs). The data store must satisfy these requirements:  
  
- Store companies and the users who work for them. Each company will have fewer than 1,000 users.  
- Some users have data larger than 2 KB.  
- Associate each user with only one company.  
- Provide the capability to browse by company.  
- Provide the capability to browse users by company.  
- Whenever a company or user profile is selected, display a details page for the company and all related users.  
- Be optimized for data reads.  
  
Which design should you implement to optimize the data store for reading data?

options.text: In a directory container, create a document for each company and a document for each user. Use the company ID as the partition key.
Create a user container that uses the user ID as the partition key and a company container that uses the company ID as the partition key. Add the company ID to each user document.
In a user container, create a document for each user. Embed the company into each user document. Use the user ID as the partition key.
In a company container, create a document for each company. Embed the users into company documents. Use the company ID as the partition key.

questions.explanation:
Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL limits an individual item to 2 MB, so embedding up to nearly 1,000 user profiles—some larger than 2 KB—in one company item is not safely supportable. Storing the company and each user as separate documents with the company ID as the partition key co-locates all related data in one logical partition. Company-centric browsing and retrieval of the company with its users can therefore be performed as efficient single-partition reads while avoiding oversized items.

**Learn more:** [Azure Cosmos DB service quotas and default limits](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/concepts-limits) · [Data modeling in Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/modeling-data)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL account with multiple write regions.  
  
You need to receive an alert when requests directed to the database exceed the available request units per second (RU/s).  
  
Which Azure Monitor signal should you use?
questions.explanation:
Azure Cosmos DB charges database operations in request units, and a request rate that exceeds provisioned RU/s is throttled. **Provisioned Throughput** is the Azure Monitor request-unit signal that represents the configured RU/s capacity; the other signals concern metadata activity, regional configuration events, or storage consumption.

You need to produce a report of the total items ordered per month, by item type. The solution must meet these requirements:

questions.explanation:
Because the source container is partitioned by `customerId`, aggregating totals by month and item type requires a cross-partition query when performed directly against orders, increasing latency and RU consumption. Maintaining that view through the Azure Cosmos DB change feed processes inserts and updates incrementally, avoiding repeated full-container daily SQL scans.

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company develops an application named App1 that uses the Azure Cosmos DB SDK with the Eventual consistency level.  
  
App1 queries an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL account named account1.  
  
You need to determine the consistency level to assign to App1 to meet these requirements:  
  
- Maximize the throughput of queries generated by App1 without increasing the number of request units currently consumed by the queries.  
- Provide the highest consistency guarantees.  
  
Which consistency level should you identify?
questions.explanation:
Session, Consistent Prefix, and Eventual are the relaxed consistency levels and provide approximately twice the read throughput of Strong and Bounded Staleness for the same request-unit capacity. The most frequent query returns the books for a specified `authorId`.

options.text: Create a container for Author and a container for Book. In each Author document, embed bookId for each book by the author. In each Book document embed authorId of each author.

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You plan to create an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL account with one write region and three read regions.  
  
You need to configure the account consistency level. The solution must satisfy these requirements:  
  
- In the write region, writes must replicate synchronously to at least three replicas.  
- In the read regions, reads must observe transactional-batch writes in order.  
- Read and write throughput must be maximized.  
  
Which consistency level should you choose?
questions.explanation:
Bounded staleness synchronously replicates writes to a local write quorum of at least three replicas and preserves write ordering for reads, subject to configured staleness bounds. Unlike Strong consistency, it does not require globally linearizable reads, enabling greater read and write throughput.

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL container.

You find that, when numerous queries run against the container, it returns an HTTP 429 error.  
  
Which two actions can reduce the number of HTTP 429 errors? Each correct answer provides a complete solution.

Add a post-trigger to the container.
Add a pre-trigger to the container.

questions.explanation:
An HTTP 429 response means Azure Cosmos DB is rate-limiting requests because their request-unit consumption exceeds the provisioned throughput. Increasing maximum throughput makes more RU/s available. Client retry logic respects the service-provided retry interval and retries throttled operations, reducing throttling failures returned to the application.

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL account named `account1`.  
  
In `account1`, you intend to create a container named `container1` to hold data collected continuously from self-driving cars. Items in `container1` will mostly be accessed through queries targeting data collected from a particular car on a given day. Each car is identified by a property named `Vehicle-Identification-Number`.  
  
You need to identify a partitioning strategy for `container1`. The strategy must meet these requirements:  
  
- Maximize read and write performance.

What should you identify?

Construct a synthetic key by concatenating the current date and a random suffix.

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to implement a trigger in the Azure Cosmos DB Core (SQL) API that executes before an item is inserted into a container.  
  
Which two actions should you take to ensure that the trigger executes? Each correct answer represents part of the solution.

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are designing an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL solution to store data from IoT devices. Device writes will occur every second, and data will be retained indefinitely.  
  
The following is a sample of the data.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1784216028396-m0hcxsh5.png)  
  
You need to choose a partition key that meets these write requirements:  
  
- Minimizes partition skew  
- Avoids capacity limits  
- Avoids hot partitions  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Create a new synthetic key that contains deviceId and timestamp.
Use timestamp as the partition key.
Use sensor1Value as the partition key.
Create a new synthetic key that contains deviceId and deviceManufacturer.

questions.explanation:
A synthetic partition key composed of `deviceId` and `timestamp` has a large number of distinct values, distributing concurrent device writes across logical partitions. Including the timestamp also limits the amount of indefinitely retained data associated with each key value, avoiding the logical-partition capacity limit. A timestamp-only key would concentrate writes occurring at the same time, while Boolean sensor data and manufacturer values have insufficient cardinality.

**Learn more:** [Choose a partition key for a real-world IoT application - Azure Cosmos DB](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/design-partitioning-iot) · [Create a synthetic partition key - Azure Cosmos DB](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/synthetic-partition-keys)

You need to ensure that, when App1 tries to delete a document in Container1, the action is blocked and an error is returned to the app.

You need to analyze the data stored in the account by using Apache Spark to build machine-learning models. The solution must **not** affect the web apps' performance.  
  
Which two actions should you take? Each correct answer represents part of the solution.  
  
**NOTE:** Each correct selection is worth one point.

options.text: In an Apache Spark pool in Azure Synapse, create a table that uses cosmos.olap as the data source.
Create a private endpoint connection to the account.
In an Azure Synapse Analytics serverless SQL pool, create a view that uses OPENROWSET and the CosmosDB provider.
Enable Azure Synapse Link for the account and Analytical store on the container.
In an Apache Spark pool in Azure Synapse, create a table that uses cosmos.oltp as the data source.

questions.explanation:
Azure Synapse Link and analytical store create a separate, isolated analytical column store for Cosmos DB data, allowing Spark analytics without affecting transactional workloads. An Azure Synapse Spark table that uses the `cosmos.olap` data source reads that analytical store; `cosmos.oltp` instead accesses the transactional store.

The `orders` container uses `customerId` as its partition key.  
  
You need to generate a report of the total items ordered per month, grouped by item type. The solution must meet these requirements:  
  
- Ensure the report runs as quickly as possible.  
- Minimize request unit (RU) consumption.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Configure the report to query orders by using a SQL query.
Configure the report to query a new aggregate container. Populate the aggregates by using the change feed.
Configure the report to query orders by using a SQL query through a dedicated gateway.
Configure the report to query a new aggregate container. Populate the aggregates by using SQL queries that run daily.

questions.explanation:
An aggregate container maintained incrementally from the Azure Cosmos DB change feed is a materialized view of the monthly, item-type totals. It avoids repeated cross-partition aggregate queries against an `orders` container partitioned by `customerId`, yielding fast report reads and lower RU consumption. Microsoft documents using the change feed to build and persist aggregated materialized views.

You have an Azure subscription containing an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL database named DB1.  
  
You develop a software-as-a-service (SaaS) app named App1 that uses DB1. App1 will be used by multiple vendors to manage their customers.  
  
You need to create a container in DB1 to store customer and order details for each vendor. The solution must meet these requirements:  
  
- Each vendor must have a unique tenant ID.  
- Container performance must be optimized for reads.  
- Customer IDs can be duplicated across the container, but they must be unique for each vendor.  
- The container must be optimized for concurrent queries from multiple customers. Each query will return data for one vendor.  
  
How should you configure the container?

options.text: Add a partition key to the tenant ID and a unique key policy to the customer ID.
Add hierarchical partition key on (tenant identifier, customer identifier).
Add a partition key to the customer ID and a unique key policy to the tenant ID.
Add hierarchical partition key on (customer identifier, tenant identifier).

questions.explanation:
A hierarchical partition key ordered as tenant identifier followed by customer identifier is suited to a read-heavy multitenant workload. The tenant identifier first allows queries filtered to a vendor to be routed only to that tenant’s relevant subpartitions, rather than fanning out across the container. The tenant/customer combination scopes customer identities within a vendor and distributes that vendor’s customer and order data across subpartitions, supporting concurrent reads.

**Learn more:** [Hierarchical partition keys in Azure Cosmos DB](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/hierarchical-partition-keys) · [Partitioning and horizontal scaling in Azure Cosmos DB](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/partitioning)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL account that includes a database named DB1.  
  
Users execute the following query against DB1:  
  
```sql  
SELECT *  
FROM c  
WHERE c.bikeParts = "Frame, Chain, Peddles"  
ORDER BY c.bikeParts ASC  
```  
  
You add an index to the recordset.  
  
You need to modify the query's `ORDER BY` syntax to optimize index usage. The solution must **not** alter the result set.  
  
Which syntax should you use?

options.text: ORDER BY c._ts ASC, c.bikeParts DESC
ORDER BY c._ts DESC, c.bikeParts ASC
ORDER BY c.bikeParts ASC, c._ts ASC
ORDER BY c.bikeParts DESC, c._ts ASC

questions.explanation:
For a query that filters one property and orders by another, Azure Cosmos DB can use a composite index when the filtered property is placed first in the `ORDER BY` clause. `c.bikeParts ASC, c._ts ASC` keeps `bikeParts` as the primary ascending sort key and adds `_ts` as a secondary key, matching the required composite ordering pattern.

**Learn more:** [Indexing policies in Azure Cosmos DB](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/index-policy) · [Overview of indexing in Azure Cosmos DB](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/index-overview)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a database in an Azure Cosmos DB Core (SQL) API account that is backed up every two hours.  
  
You need to implement a solution that supports point-in-time restore.

options.text: Enable Continuous Backup for the account.
Configure the Backup & Restore settings for the account.
Create a new account that has a periodic backup policy.
Configure the Point In Time Restore settings for the account.

questions.explanation:
Azure Cosmos DB point-in-time restore is supported by continuous backup mode. Periodic backups, including a two-hour backup interval, do not enable point-in-time restore; the account must be migrated or configured for continuous backup first.

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure subscription containing an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL account.  
  
You need to write a SQL query that returns multiple items. The solution must meet these requirements:  
  
- For every returned item, include the current Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) date and time formatted as an ISO 8601 string.  
- Minimize development effort.  
  
What should you use?
questions.explanation:
`GetCurrentDateTime()` is a built-in Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL query function that returns the current UTC date and time as an ISO 8601 string. It can be used directly in the query projection for each returned item, avoiding the additional development required for a user-defined function. `GetCurrentTimestamp()` instead returns milliseconds since the Unix epoch.

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are designing an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL solution to store data from IoT devices. The devices will write every second, and data will be retained indefinitely.  
  
The following is a sample of the data.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783849719407-74k1wwxz.png)  
  
You need to choose a partition key that meets these write requirements:  
  
- Minimizes partition skew  
- Avoids capacity limits  
- Avoids hot partitions  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Use deviceManufacturer as the partition key.
Create a new synthetic key that contains deviceId and timestamp.
Create a new synthetic key that contains deviceId and deviceManufacturer.
Use deviceId as the partition key.

questions.explanation:
A synthetic partition key that combines `deviceId` and `timestamp` has high cardinality and distributes continuous device writes across many logical partitions. The time component prevents indefinitely retained data for a device from accumulating under one partition-key value, avoiding the 20-GB logical-partition limit; the combined values also reduce skew and hot-partition risk. Microsoft documents this IoT pattern as a synthetic key combining device ID with a time-based key.

**Learn more:** [Choose a partition key for a real-world IoT application - Azure Cosmos DB](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/design-partitioning-iot) · [Create a synthetic partition key - Azure Cosmos DB](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/synthetic-partition-keys)

options.text: a composite index for (name DESC, timestamp ASC)
a composite index for (name ASC, timestamp ASC) and a composite index for (name DESC, timestamp DESC)
a composite index for (name ASC, timestamp ASC)
a composite index for (name ASC, timestamp DESC)

questions.explanation:
Azure Cosmos DB requires a composite index for an `ORDER BY` over multiple properties. A composite index on `(name ASC, timestamp ASC)` supports that property sequence in ascending order and also supports the order with every path reversed, `(name DESC, timestamp DESC)`. Thus a single composite index optimizes both query patterns while avoiding the extra write cost of maintaining a second composite index.

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure Cosmos DB Core (SQL) API account named account1 that supports an application named App1. App1 uses the consistent prefix consistency level.

You are assessing the throughput available for Container1.  
  
What is the maximum burst capacity that Container1 can accumulate?
questions.explanation:
Azure Cosmos DB burst capacity can accumulate up to 300 seconds of unused provisioned throughput for each physical partition. A single partition provisioned at 100 RU/s can therefore accumulate 100 × 300 = 30,000 RU of burst capacity.\

You need to estimate the costs of `container1` based on its current usage.  
  
How many RU/s will be charged?
questions.explanation:
Azure Cosmos DB autoscale throughput with a 20,000 RU/s maximum can scale from 2,000 to 20,000 RU/s. A 20,000 RU/s maximum supports up to 2,000 GB of storage, so 240 GB does not require the configured maximum to increase. The applicable estimate is 20,000 RU/s.\
\
**Learn more:** [Frequently Asked Questions About Autoscale Throughput - Azure Cosmos DB](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/autoscale-faq) · [Create Containers and Databases with Autoscale Throughput - Azure Cosmos DB](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/provision-throughput-autoscale)

You need to estimate the costs of `container1` based on its current usage.  
  
How many RU/s will be charged?
questions.explanation:
In Cosmos DB indexing paths, /? indexes the scalar value at a node and /* matches everything below a node; when included and excluded paths overlap, the more precise path wins. The included path /product/category/? indexes the scalar at /product/category, and although /* excludes everything, /product/category/? is more precise, so /product/category is indexed. /product/brand is explicitly listed in excludedPaths, overriding it. /product/brand/tailspin (B) is a nested child not covered by /product/brand/? (which only indexes the scalar directly at brand), and /product/[]/category (D) is array notation that appears nowhere in the policy. Thus /product/category is the indexed path.

You have an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL account that is using the default consistency level.  
  
How can you modify the consistency level as part of a query request?
questions.explanation:
Azure Cosmos DB permits a client or individual request to relax the account-level consistency setting for reads and queries. A request-level setting must be the same as or weaker than the account’s configured consistency level; it does not override write consistency or increase consistency beyond the account setting.\
\

You plan to implement an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL single-region write account named account1 that replicates across two Azure regions.  
  
You need to configure the default consistency level for account1. The solution must meet these requirements:  
  
- Writes must be performed to a local majority in one region.  
- Reads must be performed from a local minority in one region.  
  
Which consistency level should you choose?
questions.explanation:
Bounded Staleness uses local-majority writes for a single-region write account and local-minority quorum reads. Strong consistency also uses local-minority reads, but its writes require a global majority across regions, so it does not meet the local-write requirement.\

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You intend to implement an Azure Cosmos DB container to store telemetry data from 1,000 IoT devices. The data will be updated every minute. An app will read the data daily and produce aggregated reports that summarize each device’s state.  
  
You need to configure a partition key for the container. The solution must meet these requirements:  
  
- Minimize the risk of reaching partition limits.  
- Distribute read and write operations evenly across the partitions.  
- Minimize the time required to find a particular set of telemetry values.  
  
What should you set as the partition key?

options.text: the date and a random value

questions.explanation:
Device ID provides a high-cardinality key with one logical partition per device, so similarly active devices distribute storage and request-unit consumption across partitions rather than concentrating all current writes on a date-based partition. It also colocates a device’s telemetry, enabling efficient device-targeted reads for reporting. A date key concentrates concurrent writes, and a random component makes device-specific retrieval inefficient. Microsoft guidance identifies device ID as a suitable partition key for IoT workloads when devices generate similar volumes of data.

**Learn more:** [Partitioning and horizontal scaling in Azure Cosmos DB](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/partitioning) · [Data modeling in Azure Cosmos DB](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/modeling-data)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a container in an Azure Cosmos DB Core (SQL) API account that stores telemetry data from IoT devices. The container uses `telemetryId` as its partition key and has throughput of 1,000 request units per second (RU/s). About 5,000 IoT devices submit data every five minutes using the same `telemetryId` value.  
  
An application performs analytics on the data and frequently reads telemetry data for one IoT device to perform trend analysis.  
  
The following is an example document in the container.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783832325891-nn5g6nf4.png)  
  
You need to reduce the request units (RUs) consumed by the analytics application.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Decrease the offerThroughput value for the container.
Increase the offerThroughput value for the container.
Move the data to a new container that uses a partition key of deviceId.
Move the data to a new container that uses a partition key of temp.

questions.explanation:
A `deviceId` partition key has high cardinality and matches the frequent access pattern of reading one device’s telemetry. Queries filtered by that partition key can be routed to the relevant partition instead of fanning out across partitions, reducing RU consumption. A single shared `telemetryId` value does not distribute requests effectively, and changing provisioned throughput does not reduce the RU charge of the reads.

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure subscription. The subscription includes an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL account named `account1` whose default consistency level is Consistent Prefix.  
  
You run a `SELECT` query and specify the Consistent Prefix consistency level.  
  
You need to run a second `SELECT` query in the same session and specify a lower consistency level.  
  
Which consistency level can be used for the second `SELECT` query?
questions.explanation:

For how many RU/s are you charged when actual RU/s usage is zero?
questions.explanation:
Azure Cosmos DB autoscale billing has a minimum hourly charge of 10% of the configured maximum throughput (`Tmax`). A `Tmax` of 20,000 RU/s therefore has a minimum billable throughput of 2,000 RU/s, including when there are no requests.\

the consistency level of the requests from App1

questions.explanation:
The integrated cache is served only by the dedicated gateway, so the CosmosClient must connect in Gateway connectivity mode. In the current .NET and Java SDKs the default connection mode is Direct, which bypasses the gateway entirely, so every request reaches the backend and consumes RUs while both hit-rate metrics stay at 0. Since the dedicated gateway cluster is already provisioned and referenced in the connection string, the remaining fix is to set the client's connectivity mode to Gateway (choice C). Changing the consistency level (B/D) is not the issue because eventual consistency is already compatible with the integrated cache (only stronger-than-session consistency bypasses it), and the indexing policy (A) is unrelated to caching.

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You intend to store order data in an Azure Cosmos DB Core (SQL) API account. The data includes details about orders and their related items.  
  
You need to develop a model that supports order read operations. The solution must minimize the number of requests.  
  
What should you do?

Create a single database that contains a container for orders and a container for order items.
Create a single database that contains one container. Store orders and order items in separate documents in the container.
Create a single database that contains one container. Create a separate document for each order and embed the order items into the order documents.

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a container named `container1` in an Azure Cosmos DB Core (SQL) API account named `account1`, configured with the session default consistency level. The average size of an item in `contained` is 20 KB.  
  
You have an application named `App1` that uses the Azure Cosmos DB SDK and performs a point read on the same set of items in `container1` every minute.  
  
You need to minimize the request unit (RU) consumption associated with reads by `App1`.  
  
What should you do?

In App1, change the consistency level of read requests to consistent prefix
In account1, provision a dedicated gateway and integrated cache
In account1, change the default consistency level to bounded staleness

An Azure Cosmos DB dedicated gateway includes an integrated item cache for point reads. questions.explanation:
Azure Cosmos DB change-feed triggers require independent lease state for separate functions that must each process the same container updates. Assigning a different `leaseCollectionPrefix` to each function isolates its leases, while using the same `leaseCollectionName` lets the functions share one lease collection. Microsoft recommends either dedicated lease collections or distinct lease prefixes; the shared collection with distinct prefixes meets the independent-processing requirement without creating additional lease collections.

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to create a database in an Azure Cosmos DB Core (SQL) API account. The database will include three containers named coll1, coll2, and coll3. The coll1 container will have unpredictable read and write volumes. The coll2 and coll3 containers will have predictable read and write volumes. The anticipated maximum throughput for coll1 and coll2 is 50,000 request units per second (RU/s) each.  
  
How should you provision the collection while minimizing costs?

options.text: Create a provisioned throughput account. Set the throughput for coll1 to Autoscale. Set the throughput for coll2 and coll3 to Manual.
Create a provisioned throughput account. Set the throughput for coll1 to Manual. Set the throughput for coll2 and coll3 to Autoscale.

questions.explanation:
Azure Cosmos DB autoscale provisioned throughput is intended for variable or unpredictable workloads and can scale to a configured maximum of 50,000 RU/s. Manual provisioned throughput is appropriate for predictable, stable workloads. A provisioned throughput account with autoscale for coll1 and manual throughput for coll2 and coll3 therefore minimizes cost while meeting the workload requirements. Serverless is not appropriate for this sustained high-throughput requirement.

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You plan to create an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL database named `db1` that will have two containers. One container will store blog posts, and the other will store users. Every item in the blog post container will include:

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a database named `db1` in an Azure Cosmos DB Core (SQL) API account called `account1`.  
  
You need to write JSON data to `db1` by using Azure Stream Analytics. The solution must minimize costs.  
  
What should you do before you can use `db1` as a Stream Analytics output?

options.text: In account1, add a private endpoint
In db1, create containers that have a custom indexing policy and analytical store disabled
In db1, create containers that have an automatic indexing policy and analytical store enabled
In account1, enable a dedicated gateway

questions.explanation:
Azure Stream Analytics requires the target Azure Cosmos DB containers to exist before they can be used as an output. A custom indexing policy can reduce RU consumption from indexing during writes, and disabling analytical store avoids the additional analytical-store replication and storage costs when it is not required.

**Learn more:** [Azure Stream Analytics output to Azure Cosmos DB](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/stream-analytics/stream-analytics-documentdb-output) · [Indexing policies in Azure Cosmos DB](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/index-policy)

questions.domain: Optimize an Azure Cosmos DB solution
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL database hosting a container named Container1. Container1 stores product details.  
  
You have a query named Query1 that contains the following statements.  
  
```sql  
SELECT p.ProductGroup, p.Color  
FROM products AS p  
WHERE p.ProductName = "100mm Return Valve"  
  AND p.ListPrice > 120  
```  
  
You need to optimize Query1 performance by using custom indexing.  
  
Which set of index components will optimize Query1?

options.text: ListPrice DESC, ProductName ASC, ProductGroup ASC, Color ASC
ListPrice ASC, ProductName ASC, ProductGroup ASC, Color ASC

questions.explanation:
A composite index for filters on multiple properties places equality-filter properties first and the single range-filter property last. `ProductName` is an equality filter and `ListPrice` is a greater-than range filter, so a composite index ordered as `ProductName, ListPrice` optimizes the query. The ascending or descending direction does not affect composite-index optimization for these filters. [Indexing policies - Azure Cosmos DB](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/index-policy)

**Learn more:** [Indexing policies - Azure Cosmos DB](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/index-policy)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You must implement a solution for the planned changes while meeting the product catalog requirements.  
  
What should you do to implement the conflict-resolution policy?

options.text: Set the default consistency level for account1 to eventual
Remove frequently changed fields from the index policy of the con-product container
Create a new container and migrate the product catalog data to the new container
Disable indexing on all fields in the index policy of the con-product container

questions.explanation:
An Azure Cosmos DB container’s conflict-resolution policy can be specified only at container creation and cannot be changed afterward. Implementing a new required policy therefore requires creating a new container configured with that policy and migrating the product catalog data to it.

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are developing an application that will store data in an Azure Cosmos DB Core (SQL) API account. The account uses the session default consistency level. Five other applications also use the account. The account has one read-write region and 10 additional read regions.  
  
Approximately 20 percent of the items stored in the account are updated every hour.  
  
Several users will use the new application from multiple devices.  
  
You need to ensure that users consistently see the same item values when browsing from different devices. The solution must **NOT** affect the other applications.  
  
Which two actions should you take? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.  
  
**NOTE:** Each correct selection is worth one point.

options.text: Set the default consistency level to eventual
Associate a session token to the device
Use implicit session management when performing read requests
Provide a stored session token when performing read requests
Associate a session token to the user account

questions.explanation:
Azure Cosmos DB session consistency uses session tokens to ensure reads do not return an older version than the one already observed in that session. To preserve this guarantee across multiple devices, persist the relevant session token with the user account and provide that token on subsequent read requests. Implicit token management applies only within an SDK client instance, while changing the account default consistency level would affect all applications using the account.

**Learn more:** [Manage consistency levels in Azure Cosmos DB](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/nosql/how-to-manage-consistency) · [Consistency levels in Azure Cosmos DB](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/consistency-levels)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a database named `db1` in an Azure Cosmos DB Core (SQL) API account.  
  
You are designing an application that will use `db1`. In `db1`, you are creating a new container named `coll1` to store online orders. The following is a sample document that will be stored in `coll1`.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783832098544-404sr11z.png)  
  
The application will have these characteristics:  
  
- New orders will be created frequently by different customers.  
- Customers will often view their previous order history.  
  
You need to choose the partition key value for `coll1` to support the application. The solution must minimize costs.  
  
To what should you set the partition key?
questions.explanation:
Using `customerId` as the partition key groups each customer’s orders in the same logical partition. Queries for a customer’s order history can therefore be routed to the relevant partition instead of fanning out across partitions, which reduces request-unit consumption and cost. Microsoft recommends a high-cardinality partition key that matches query filters, specifically citing `CustomerId` for retrieving all orders for a customer.

**Learn more:** [Partitioning and horizontal scaling in Azure Cosmos DB](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/partitioning) · [Query an Azure Cosmos DB container](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/how-to-query-container)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have the following query.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783812040009-vf68doo1.png)  
  
You must recommend a composite-index strategy that minimizes the request units (RUs) consumed by the query. What should you recommend?

options.text: a composite index for (sensor ASC, value ASC) and a composite index for (sensor ASC, timestamp ASC)
a composite index for (sensor ASC, value ASC, timestamp ASC) and a composite index for (sensor DESC, value DESC, timestamp DESC)
a composite index for (value ASC, sensor ASC) and a composite index for (timestamp ASC, sensor ASC)
a composite index for (sensor ASC, value ASC, timestamp ASC)

questions.explanation:
Azure Cosmos DB can use a composite index to optimize an equality filter together with one range filter. A composite index can optimize at most one range filter, and equality-filter properties must be listed first. Because `value < 22` and `timestamp >= 1619146031231` are separate range filters following the equality filter on `sensor`, the efficient strategy uses `(sensor ASC, value ASC)` and `(sensor ASC, timestamp ASC)`.

**Learn more:** [Indexing policies - Azure Cosmos DB](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/index-policy)

questions.question:
You have an Azure subscription containing an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL account named account1. The account uses strong consistency and is deployed in the East US, West US, and Central US Azure regions.  
  
The round-trip time (RTT) between these regions is shown in the following table.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783905263312-cc6nt08v.png)  
  
What write latency should you estimate for write requests to account1?
questions.explanation:
For an Azure Cosmos DB account that uses strong consistency across multiple regions, write latency is estimated as twice the RTT between the two farthest regions, plus 10 ms at the 99th percentile. East US and West US are farthest apart at 136 ms, so the estimate is 2 × 136 ms + 10 ms = 282 ms.\
\
**Learn more:** [Consistency levels in Azure Cosmos DB](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/consistency-levels)

What write latency should you estimate for write requests to account1?

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a container named `container1` in an Azure Cosmos DB Core (SQL) API account.  
  
You need to grant a user named `User1` the ability to insert items into `container1` by using role-based access control (RBAC). The solution must follow the principle of least privilege.  
  
Which role should you assign to `User1`?

Cosmos DB Built-in Data Contributor only

The Cosmos DB Built-in Data Contributor role grants Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL data-plane permissions for item operations, including creating items. CosmosDB Operator and DocumentDB Account Contributor are management-plane roles; they do not grant the necessary data-plane permission to insert items. Assigning only the data contributor role satisfies the required access without unnecessary account-management permissions.

You have a third-party application exposed through a REST API.  
  
You need to migrate data from the application to a container in `db1` each week.  
  
What should you use?

questions.question:
You have a database named `db1` in an Azure Cosmos DB Core (SQL) API account.  
  
You have a third-party application exposed through a REST API.  
  
You need to migrate data from the application to a container in `db1` each week.  
  
What should you use?

options.text: Update the document of each family member separately by using a patch operation
Update the document of each family member separately and set the consistency level to strong
Update the document of each family member by using a transactional batch operation

questions.explanation:
Azure Cosmos DB transactional batch operations provide full ACID transactions for point operations within the same logical partition key. Because all affected family-member documents share `familyId`, their address updates can be submitted in one transactional batch, so they either all commit or all roll back. Sending the operations in a single request also reduces latency compared with separate updates.

**Learn more:** [Transactional batch operations in Azure Cosmos DB](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/transactional-batch)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure subscription.  
  
You plan to create an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL database named DB1 to store author and book data for authors who have each published up to ten books. Typical, frequent data queries will include:  
  
- All books written by an individual author  
- The synopsis of individual books  
  
You need to recommend a data model for DB1. The solution must meet these requirements:  
  
- Support transactional updates to the author and book data.  
- Minimize read operation costs.  
  
What should you recommend?

options.text: Create a single container that stores author items and book items, and then items that represent the relationship between the authors and their books.
Create three containers, one that stores author items, a second that stores book items, and a third that stores items that represent the relationship between the authors and their books.
Create two containers, one that stores author items and another that stores book items. Embed a list of each author’s books in the corresponding author item.
Create a single container that stores author items and book items. Embed a list of each author’s books in the corresponding author item.

questions.explanation:
Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL provides ACID transactional operations only within the same logical partition of a single container. Keeping author and book items in one container enables transactional updates when related items share the author partition key. Embedding the small, bounded book list in its author item serves the frequent all-books-by-author access pattern with a single read, while individual book items support direct synopsis retrieval. [Transactional batch operations — Azure Cosmos DB](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/transactional-batch)

**Learn more:** [Transactional batch operations — Azure Cosmos DB](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/transactional-batch)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are designing an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL solution to store data from IoT devices. Device writes will occur every second, and the data will be retained indefinitely.  
  
The following is a sample of the data.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1784216039260-sgysl8vz.png)  
  
You need to choose a partition key that meets these write requirements:  
  
- Minimizes partition skew  
- Avoids capacity limits  
- Avoids hot partitions  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Use deviceId as the partition key.
Create a new Synthetic key that contains deviceId and deviceManufacturer.
Use deviceManufacturer as the partition key.
Create a new synthetic key that contains deviceId and a random number.

questions.explanation:
A synthetic partition key made from `deviceId` plus a random number spreads each device’s continuous writes and indefinitely retained records across multiple logical partitions. This provides more even distribution, avoids concentrating a high-write device in a hot partition, and prevents a single device key from accumulating all of that device’s data toward a logical-partition capacity limit.

**Learn more:** [Create a synthetic partition key - Azure Cosmos DB](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/synthetic-partition-keys) · [Choose a partition key for a real-world IoT application - Azure Cosmos DB](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/design-partitioning-iot)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure Cosmos DB account that contains one container named Container1. Container1 stores items with two properties: TenantId and UserId. Container1 uses the TenantId property for logical partitioning.  
  
You need to configure subpartitioning for Container1 by using the UserId property. The solution must maximize data availability.  
  
What should you do first?

options.text: Enable the analytical store for Container1.

questions.explanation:
Azure Cosmos DB hierarchical partition keys must be defined when a container is created; an existing partition-key definition cannot be modified in place. Creating a new container configured with TenantId and UserId as hierarchical partition keys enables data to be migrated while the original container remains available.

questions.question:
You have an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL database that contains a container named Container1.  
  
For Container1, the `DefaultTimeToLive` property is set to `-1`.  
  
You add an item to Container1 whose `ttl` property is `1000`.  
  
When will the item be automatically deleted?

options.text: one second after the item is last accessed
1,000 seconds after the item is last accessed
1,000 seconds after the item is last modified

questions.explanation:
A container `DefaultTimeToLive` value of `-1` enables TTL without a default expiration, while a positive item-level `ttl` overrides it. The `ttl` value is a number of seconds measured from the item's last-modified timestamp; therefore, the item expires after 1,000 seconds following its last modification.\
\
**Learn more:** [Expire data with time to live in Azure Cosmos DB](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/time-to-live)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building a web app named App1 that will store customer-created content in an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL database named DB1.  
  
You configure an Azure AI Search indexer to automatically import documents from DB1 into an Azure AI Search index.  
  
App1 uses REST APIs to deliver advanced search and retrieval functionality for the documents.  
  
You need to determine the query types that can be used in Azure AI Search to retrieve text data. The solution must minimize development effort.  
  
Which three query types can you use? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are designing an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL solution to store IoT-device data. Device writes will occur every second, and data will be retained indefinitely.  
  
The following is a sample of the data.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1786539227527-qmfum5te.png)  
  
You need to choose a partition key that meets these write requirements:  
  
- Minimizes partition skew  
- Avoids capacity limits  
- Avoids hot partitions  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Create a new synthetic key that contains deviceId and timestamp.
Use deviceId as the partition key.
Use deviceManufacturer as the partition key.
Create a new synthetic key that contains deviceId and sensor1Value.

questions.explanation:
A synthetic partition key composed of `deviceId` and `timestamp` has high cardinality and spreads each device’s continuous writes across many logical partitions. This prevents one device’s indefinitely retained data from accumulating in a single logical partition, which avoids the 20-GB logical-partition limit and reduces the risk of hot partitions. Microsoft’s IoT partitioning guidance specifically identifies a synthetic key combining device ID with a granular time-based value as a way to distribute writes and avoid that limit.

questions.question:
You have an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL account that contains a container named Container1.  
  
You implement a change feed processor.  
  
You determine that the processor is handling changes more slowly than changes occur in Container1.  
  
You need to resolve the issue.  
  
What should you use?

options.text: Add a pre-trigger to the blog post container.
Create a duplicate of each user item in the blog post container.
Add a pre-trigger to the user container.
Create a duplicate of each blog post item in the user container.

questions.explanation:
A duplicate of each blog post item in the user container places the posts for a user in the logical partition keyed by that user's ID. A posts-by-user query can therefore include an equality filter on the partition key and run in-partition, avoiding the higher RU cost of a fan-out query against the post-ID-partitioned container. Azure Cosmos DB guidance specifically uses denormalized post items in a user-ID-partitioned users container to optimize listing a user’s posts.

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL database that contains the containers shown in the following table.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1786539228186-8deoahun.png)  
  
You need to ensure that when a product name is changed in the Products container, the product name is updated in every order that has **not** been shipped.  
  
What should you implement?
questions.explanation:
Azure Cosmos DB change feed records item updates in a container and can drive asynchronous processing that updates denormalized data in another container. Server-side triggers and stored procedures are limited to a single container and logical partition, so they cannot propagate a Products update to the separate OrderItems container. Microsoft documents change feed as the pattern for denormalized replication across containers.

**Learn more:** [Change Feed Design Patterns - Azure Cosmos DB](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/change-feed-design-patterns) · [Write Stored Procedures, Triggers, and UDFs - Azure Cosmos DB](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/nosql/how-to-write-stored-procedures-triggers-udfs)

questions.question:
You have an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL account called account1.  
  
You have an app named App1 that connects to account1 and uses strong consistency for every request.  
  
You implement the Azure Cosmos DB integrated cache for account1.  
  
You need to ensure that App1 uses the integrated cache.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Change the request consistency level to session.
Change the request consistency level to bounded staleness.
Set the connectivity mode to direct mode over TCP.

questions.explanation:
Azure Cosmos DB integrated cache supports read requests using only session or eventual consistency. Reads using strong consistency bypass the integrated cache and are served from the backend, so App1 must use session consistency for its requests to use the cache.\
\

questions.question:
You have an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL account called account1.  
  
You have an app named App1 that connects to account1 and uses strong consistency for every request.  
  
You implement the Azure Cosmos DB integrated cache for account1.  
  
You need to ensure that App1 uses the integrated cache.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Use an UPDATE instead of a DELETE.
Add an IsDeleted flag to the items.

questions.explanation:
The default latest-version change feed does not capture direct delete operations. A soft-delete design adds an `IsDeleted` flag and updates that flag instead of physically deleting the item; the update is emitted through the change feed, allowing the cache to remove or invalidate the customer. Microsoft Learn identifies a soft-delete marker as the common approach for handling deletes in latest-version mode.

**Learn more:** [Change feed modes in Azure Cosmos DB](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/change-feed-modes) · [Change Feed Design Patterns - Azure Cosmos DB](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/nosql/change-feed-design-patterns)

Container1 includes an item with a `ttl` property of 1000.  
  
The item in Container1 is modified.

You have an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL account that includes a database and a container named Container1. You plan to develop a new app named App1 that will store entities in Container1. App1 must meet the following entity-versioning requirements:  
  
- Each entity must be associated with multiple document versions.  
- Each document version must be associated with one entity.  
  
You need to recommend a versioning model for App1. The solution must minimize development and operational effort.  
  
What should you recommend?

options.text: Use a single document model that contains all the versions of an entity as a value in a root property.
Use a multiple document model that stores each version of an entity as a separate document. Each document will include the data for all the entities in that version.
Use a multiple document model that contains all the versions of an entity as separate documents in a collection.
Use a single document model that contains all the entities as a value in a root property.

questions.explanation:
A one-to-many relationship between an entity and its document versions is best represented by separate version documents that each carry a reference to their single parent entity. This avoids a mutable, growing array of versions in one item and aligns with Azure Cosmos DB guidance to keep one-to-many children as separate items when growth can be unbounded.

**Learn more:** [Data modeling in Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/modeling-data)

User permissions are associated with a user and will **not** be queried separately from that user.  
  
Product price is associated with a product and will **not** be queried separately from that product.  
  
You are designing a new data model for DB1.  
  
You need to optimize the data model to improve read performance and maintainability. The solution must meet these requirements:  
  
- Future enhancements to user permissions must be supported.  
- Future enhancements to product price do **not** need to be supported.  
  
Which two actions should you take? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.  
  
> **NOTE:** Each correct selection is worth one point.

options.text: Create a new container to store both the product information and the product price in separate documents and link the documents by using a shared product ID.
Denormalize the product price into product documents in Container3.
Denormalize the user permissions into user documents in Container1.
Denormalize user documents into the user permissions in Container2.
Denormalize product documents into the product price in Container4.
Store both the user information and the user permissions in a single container in separate documents that have references.

questions.explanation:
Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL commonly improves read performance by denormalizing contained data that is read together into one item. Because product price is always read with its product and requires no future enhancement, embed the price in each product document. User permissions are likewise always read with their user, so embed the permissions in the user document; the JSON document can be extended with additional permission properties as future requirements arise. This design avoids separate-document lookups for both access patterns.

**Learn more:** [Data modeling in Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/modeling-data)

options.text: Embed the order lines of each order in the same container.
Store the orders in a separate container from the order lines.
Store individual orders and order lines as separate items in the same container. Normalize the items to minimize their size.
Store individual orders and individual order lines as separate items in the same container. Include a type attribute in each item.

questions.explanation:
For a contained, one-to-few relationship whose data is commonly retrieved together, Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL recommends embedding the child data in the parent item. Storing an order and its lines in one item enables a single read rather than multiple item reads or queries, which improves read performance and lowers request-unit consumption.

options.text: For DB1, set Throughput to Autoscale.
Configure the indexing policy to include only int1 and exclude string1, string2, and string3.
Configure the indexing policy to include only int1 and exclude all other attributes.

questions.explanation:
An indexing policy that includes only `int1` and excludes all other attributes reduces index maintenance and storage, lowering write RU consumption. The `int1` partition-key property must be indexed to efficiently serve a query that filters on it; `string1`, `string2`, and `string3` are only returned by the query and do not need indexes. Microsoft Learn documents that optimizing indexed paths can substantially reduce write latency and RU charges, and that a partition-key property should be explicitly included when using an opt-in indexing policy.

Which two operations can the Copy activity carry out? Each correct answer provides a complete solution.  
  
NOTE: Each correct answer is worth one point.
questions.explanation:
For an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL sink, Azure Data Factory Copy activity supports `insert` and `upsert` write behaviors. An upsert replaces a document with the same ID when it exists; otherwise, it inserts a new document. The connector does not expose update, delete, or truncate as Copy activity write behaviors.
